one_liner: Pure-Julia 2D/spherical geometry ops; beats GEOS-through-GeoPandas/R on simple point tasks, but trails GEOS called directly.
what_it_does: GeometryOps.jl is a Julia package of planar and spherical geometry operations (OGC predicates, distance, area, centroid, clipping, simplify, segmentize, convex hull, polygonize, reprojection through Proj.jl) that accepts any GeoInterface.jl-compatible geometry, plus apply/applyreduce for mapping over nested geometries and tables. Operations take an optional algorithm or manifold as the first argument (Planar(), Spherical(), Geodesic(); FosterHormannClipping, the experimental OverlayNG and RelateNG engines, GEOS() and TG() backends). It is not a GEOS binding or drop-in: it has its own Julia API, and some operations (buffer) simply call GEOS through LibGEOS.jl.
how_it_is_fast: Julia compiles each call specialised to the concrete geometry and coordinate types (plain tuples after GO.tuples), so tight loops such as point-to-point distance or point-in-polygon have no per-row interpreter or wrapper marshalling cost. Clipping uses Foster-Hormann with selectable edge-intersection accelerators (NestedLoop, single/dual STRtree, natural-index trees, AutoAccelerator), and the newer OverlayNG/RelateNG ports of the JTS algorithms use exact adaptive predicates plus a prepared, indexed point-in-area locator (GO.prepare). There is no GEOS-beating kernel algorithm: the third-party wins come from avoiding Python/R per-row overhead on simple point tasks.
when_to_use: You already work in Julia and want generic geometry operations over GeoInterface types (GeoDataFrames, Shapefile, GeoJSON, ArchGDAL objects) without converting to GEOS.

Bulk simple point workloads (pairwise point distances, many points against one polygon, rejection sampling inside a polygon) where kadyb/vector-benchmark measured 0.11 s vs 0.9 s (GeoPandas) and 0.04 s vs 0.12 s / 0.08 s (GeoPandas / R geos).
Many repeated point-in-polygon queries against one large polygon, using GO.prepare (1.2 us per query on Canada vs 62.6 us unprepared in its own benchmark).
Spherical-manifold predicates and overlays (great-circle edges) that GEOS does not offer, accepting about 5-11x the planar cost.
Points x area overlays (union/symdifference of a MultiPoint with a polygon), the one case its own benchmark shows ahead of LibGEOS (2.4 ms vs 20.6 ms).
when_not_to_use: From C++: it is Julia-only and needs an embedded Julia runtime, so for a C++ project call GEOS, TG or Boost.Geometry directly.

Polygon overlay throughput: its own benchmark (Apple M4 Pro, Julia 1.12.6, GEOS 3.14.1) has OverlayNG 2-4x slower than LibGEOS on country pairs and about 30x slower on river x country intersection; issue #129 reports Foster-Hormann clipping more than 10x slower than LibGEOS above about 100 vertices.
Pairwise predicate filtering of mostly disjoint polygons: RelateNG takes 1.6 us per pair vs 115.7 ns for LibGEOS (about 14x behind).

Union/difference on MultiPolygon inputs with the default Foster-Hormann engine, which raises MethodError per the project's benchmark notes; the OverlayNG alternative is marked experimental and has a known ring-assembly defect cluster.

Production code that needs a stable API: the README warns it is 'still under heavy development', the version is 0.1.x, and open bug issues cover clipping on barely touching or coverage-like polygons (#281, #337), difference (#335) and touches (#155).

integration.form: module (Julia package, registered as GeometryOps; core types in the GeometryOpsCore subpackage)
integration.dependencies: GeoInterface, GeometryOpsCore, ExactPredicates, AdaptivePredicates, DelaunayTriangulation, SortTileRecursiveTree, StaticArrays, Tables, DataAPI, Extents, GeoFormatTypes, CoordinateTransformations, AbstractTrees, PrecompileTools; optional extensions for LibGEOS (buffer and GEOS backend), Proj (reprojection), TGGeometry (libtg predicates), DataFrames, DimensionalData, FlexiJoins, Makie
integration.platforms: any platform Julia supports (pure Julia); buffer needs LibGEOS.jl and reprojection needs Proj.jl, both binary artifacts
integration.thread_safety: apply/applyreduce-based operations take a `threaded` keyword (default false) to parallelise over sub-geometries or table rows; thread safety of concurrent calls is not otherwise documented

gotchas: GO.buffer always delegates to GEOS (LibGEOS must be loaded), so its vector-benchmark buffer time (5.75 s vs 4.07 s GeoPandas) is GEOS against GEOS.

The third-party wins compare different strategies: GeoPandas distance runs a Python-level apply loop over 5,000 rows and GeoPandas intersects uses a cached STRtree sindex query, while GeometryOps brute-forces a Julia comprehension/broadcast after JIT warm-up.
Unprepared predicates recompute extents on every call; GO.tuples(x; calc_extent = true) or GO.prepare change point-in-area cost from 62.6 us to 21.9 us or 1.2 us per query.
Foster-Hormann returns a list of geometries, while OverlayNG returns a single most-specific geometry (possibly mixed-dimension), so switching engines changes result shapes.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick it over TG or qdgeo only when you are in Julia and want GeoInterface-generic, planar plus spherical operations in one package; for raw predicate speed TG is faster than GEOS prepared, and GeometryOps can even call it through GO.TG(). Arctern and qdgeo target the same GeoPandas/Shapely baseline from C++/GPU or Rust/WASM and are the better fit outside Julia.
verified_claims_summary: Third-party kadyb/vector-benchmark (Ryzen 9 5900X, Ubuntu 22.04, median of runs; no Julia/R/Python versions) shows GeometryOps ahead of GEOS-through-wrappers on three point tasks: distance on a 5,000 x 5,000 point matrix 0.11 s vs 0.9 s (GeoPandas) and 5.37 s (R geos, row-wise sapply), 500,000 points-in-polygon intersects 0.04 s vs 0.12 s / 0.08 s, and sampling 0.04 s vs 0.9 s. The project's own direct comparison against LibGEOS (GEOS 3.14.1, Apple M4 Pro) shows it slower than GEOS on predicates and overlays except points x area unions.
status_note: Actively developed (last commit 2026-09-20, 488 commits, about 135 open issues and 44 open PRs) and MIT-licensed, but explicitly in-development 0.1.x software usable only from Julia.
